sources.title: The Next Revolution: Popular Assemblies and the Promise of Direct Democracy
sources.author: Murray Bookchin

sources.title: The Politics of Social Ecology: Libertarian Municipalism
sources.author: Janet Biehl (with Murray Bookchin)

archetypes.name: Anarcho-capitalism
archetypes.summary: Prioritises absolute self-ownership, private property and voluntary contract over any state. Even law, security and defence would be supplied by competing private firms in a free market.
archetypes.signature: ideal: stateless private-law society; now: radical deregulation, tax resistance, crypto and exit strategies
archetypes.brief: The non-aggression principle is the foundation: no one may initiate force against another person or their property. The state is a territorial monopoly on force financed by taxation, which is theft, so it is illegitimate. Law, courts, policing and defence can be provided by competing private agencies, insurers and arbitrators under polycentric law. Decisions are made by owners and contracts, not by votes. Democracy has no special legitimacy. Liberty is maximal, and security is a service you buy. All property is private, and free markets coordinate everything, including money. Trade is entirely free. There is no nation-state and no foreign policy, and defence is decentralised and private. Migration happens through property owners' invitation, and we are divided between open-borders and covenant-community views. There is no state religion and no state moral code: communities may set their own rules by contract. We are strongly pro-technology, enhancement and innovation.
archetypes.now_notes: Here and now the adherent supports any cut in state power: abolishing taxes and agencies, legalising drugs and all consensual acts, ending central banking, embracing cryptocurrency, homeschooling, private cities and charter zones, and non-intervention abroad. They often favour exit and agorism, the counter-economy, over electoral politics.

sources.title: For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto
sources.author: Murray N. Rothbard

archetypes.name: Anarcho-primitivism
archetypes.summary: Prioritises dismantling civilisation itself, including agriculture, industry, mass society and domestication, in favour of small, egalitarian, foraging-style communities living in wild nature, over technological progress and any form of the state.
archetypes.signature: ideal: small autonomous foraging bands in rewilded nature; now: rewilding, resistance to industrial projects, simple living
archetypes.brief: Hierarchy, the state, patriarchy and alienation did not begin with capitalism. They began with domestication and agriculture, which produced surplus, property, division of labour and rulers. Industrial civilisation is ecologically suicidal and spiritually deadening. The ideal is small, face-to-face bands and tribes living in wild nature, making decisions informally and by consensus, with no state, police or rulers. Nothing is owned beyond personal possessions. Sharing and gift replace both markets and planning. Trade is minimal and local. There are no nations, no borders and no armies, though we are divided over the morality of sabotage. People come and go freely between small groups. Organised religion is a tool of domination, though many feel animist kinship with nature. Gender roles and norms are fluid and egalitarian. We reject technology as a system: we oppose genetic engineering, AI and life extension, and even symbolic culture is questioned by some of us.
archetypes.now_notes: Here and now the adherent supports rewilding, protecting wilderness and Indigenous land rights, resisting mines, pipelines and dams, and opposing genetic engineering and AI. They practise primitive skills and low-tech living. They seldom engage in electoral politics and see reform as prolonging industrial civilisation.

archetypes.name: Absolute monarchism
archetypes.summary: Prioritises undivided sovereign authority vested in a hereditary monarch, answerable to God and conscience rather than to parliaments or voters, over popular sovereignty, divided powers and party politics.
archetypes.signature: ideal: hereditary sovereign with undivided authority; now: support for strong executive authority, restoration movements and respect for crown institutions
archetypes.brief: Sovereignty cannot be divided. A commonwealth needs one final authority to keep the peace, and a hereditary monarch serves this best. They are raised for the role, above faction, invested in the realm's long-term good, and succession is clear. The king is father of the people, bound by divine and natural law and by conscience, but not by parliaments or elections. Councils advise but do not command. Authority is centralised in the crown, though provinces and estates may keep customary privileges by royal grant. Order and security are the first goods, because without them there is no liberty. Property is secure under the king's law. The economy is guided by the crown's interest in prosperity, historically by mercantilist means. The realm's sovereignty is absolute, and the crown maintains strong forces for defence and dynastic interest. Subjects of many peoples can be loyal to one throne, and loyalty matters more than ethnicity. The established church upholds the monarch's sacred authority. Traditional family and social hierarchy are affirmed. Technology is neutral if it serves the realm. We are divided over the degree of religious foundation.
archetypes.now_notes: In a liberal democracy the adherent supports restoration or strengthening of royal prerogatives where a monarchy exists, a strong executive over parliaments and parties, an established church, traditional social order and tough law and order. They are sceptical of party democracy, and many engage culturally rather than electorally.

sources.title: Politics Drawn from the Very Words of Holy Scripture
sources.author: Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet

archetypes.name: Constitutional monarchism
archetypes.summary: Prioritises a hereditary head of state above party politics, as a symbol of continuity and national unity, over an elected presidency, while real governing power rests with an elected parliament under constitutional law.
archetypes.signature: constant
archetypes.brief: The monarch reigns but does not rule. A hereditary head of state stands above party politics. They embody the nation's history and unity, they are a neutral guardian of the constitution, and they deny any politician the highest symbolic place. The monarch has the right to be consulted, to encourage and to warn, with reserve powers for genuine constitutional crises. Governing power belongs to an elected parliament and a responsible cabinet, under the rule of law. The crown suits both unitary and federal realms, and devolution is a matter for parliament. We value liberal democracy, civil liberties and gradual constitutional evolution. On economics we span the mainstream, from market-oriented to social democratic. Trade policy likewise follows mainstream opinion and is generally open. Sovereignty rests in the crown-in-parliament, and international cooperation is welcome. The armed forces owe loyalty to the crown, which keeps them out of politics. Newcomers become subjects or citizens of the realm under one crown. Some realms keep an established church, others are secular. Social norms are moderate and traditional in ceremony. Technology is not a monarchist question. We are divided over established religion and the scope of reserve powers.
archetypes.now_notes: Here and now the adherent supports keeping the monarchy and its constitutional role, ceremonial traditions, a parliamentary system, the stability and continuity it provides, and its unifying symbolism. They oppose republican campaigns and are otherwise moderate and mainstream on policy.

sources.title: Principles of Politics Applicable to All Representative Governments
sources.author: Benjamin Constant

archetypes.name: Technocracy
archetypes.summary: Prioritises governance by qualified experts using scientific evidence and data over electoral competition, ideology and popular opinion. Policy is treated as a problem of optimal design.
archetypes.signature: ideal: expert-run planning and administration with limited electoral input; now: independent expert agencies, evidence-based policy and epistocratic reforms
archetypes.brief: Most public problems are technical: energy, health, infrastructure, the economy, climate. They should be solved by those who understand them. Engineers, scientists and trained administrators, chosen by competence, should make the key decisions, guided by data, modelling and measurable outcomes. Elections and partisan politics introduce ignorance, short-termism and demagoguery, so voters' role should be limited, with input but not control. Authority should sit at whatever level matches the technical problem, which in practice favours national and continental agencies. Liberty matters instrumentally, but rational order and public safety come first. The ownership question is pragmatic, whatever works. The economy should be steered by planning and expert agencies, using markets as tools where they perform. Trade policy should follow economic modelling, generally favouring openness while managing supply-chain risks. We support global coordination and international bodies on technical issues. Force is for rational defence only. Migration should be managed by labour-market and demographic needs. The state is strictly secular and evidence-based. Social norms should follow evidence, which is usually liberal. We strongly embrace transformative technology. We are divided between hard technocrats, who would replace politics, and soft technocrats or epistocrats, who would insulate expert bodies within democracy.
archetypes.now_notes: Here and now the adherent supports independent expert agencies (central banks, health and climate authorities, infrastructure commissions), evidence-based policy units, depoliticised civil services, AI and data-driven governance, and science funding. Some support voter-competence ideas such as epistocracy, and some support supranational technical regulation.

sources.title: The Engineers and the Price System
sources.author: Thorstein Veblen

sources.title: Technocracy Study Course
sources.author: Technocracy Inc. (M. King Hubbert et al.)

archetypes.name: Confucian meritocracy
archetypes.summary: Prioritises rule by virtuous and capable officials selected by merit, benevolent government for the people's welfare, and social harmony over competitive electoral democracy and individualist rights.
archetypes.signature: ideal: meritocratic, benevolent government with consultative input; now: civil-service excellence, family policy and moral education
archetypes.brief: Government exists for the people's welfare: the people are the root of the state. But governing well takes virtue and wisdom, so officials should be selected and promoted by examination and proven performance, not by popularity. The ideal is benevolent rule by cultivated, morally exemplary officials, with consultation and remonstrance, and with democratic input at local levels. A unified central government is the norm, with responsibilities delegated to capable local officials. Harmony, order and the family come before individual rights claims, though rulers who lose the people's trust lose their mandate. The economy is a mix: markets with state guidance, light taxes, and duties to relieve poverty. Trade is welcome where it serves the people's welfare. We prefer peaceful relations and moral influence over conquest, with defence when needed. States are sovereign, though some adherents envision 'all under heaven' (tianxia), a harmonious order beyond rival nation-states. Newcomers are welcome to adopt the culture and its rituals. Confucianism is an ethical tradition: some want it publicly honoured, others a secular state. Filial piety, ritual propriety and family obligations are central, and gender roles are traditionally hierarchical, which modern adherents debate. Technology serves the people's welfare. We are divided over Jiang Qing's tricameral Confucian constitution versus democratic-compatible Confucianism.
archetypes.now_notes: In a liberal democracy the adherent supports a highly qualified, competitive civil service, long-term planning bodies, moral and civic education, family support and elder care, consultative bodies of experts alongside elected chambers, and courteous public culture. Some favour limits on populism, such as meritocratic upper chambers.

sources.title: The China Model: Political Meritocracy and the Limits of Democracy
sources.author: Daniel A. Bell

sources.title: Confucian Perfectionism: A Political Philosophy for Modern Times
sources.author: Joseph Chan

archetypes.name: Developmental authoritarianism
archetypes.summary: Prioritises rapid economic development, stability and national strength, delivered by a strong, meritocratic state that guides private enterprise, over political pluralism, civil liberties and unrestricted markets.
archetypes.signature: ideal: dominant-party developmental state with disciplined industrial policy; now: industrial policy, order and long-term state capacity within democracy
archetypes.brief: Development first. A poor or vulnerable nation needs stability, discipline and long-term planning more than adversarial party politics. A strong executive and a dominant party or leadership should set national goals. Power is centralised in the national government, with local authorities implementing national plans. Elections may exist but must not paralyse government. A meritocratic, well-paid, incorruptible bureaucracy steers the economy. Private firms compete, but the state guides investment, credit and industrial priorities and disciplines firms through export targets. Security and order come before civil liberties: strict laws, firm policing, limits on destabilising speech. Trade is outward-oriented, with exports welcome, but infant industries are protected and capital controlled. National sovereignty is jealously guarded, and strong defence and national service are expected. Ethnic and religious groups are managed for harmony, with a shared national identity. Religion is kept out of politics, and faiths are respected. Social norms emphasise family, work ethic, thrift and communal values. We are strongly pro-science and pro-technology. We are divided on how fast to liberalise politically once development is achieved.
archetypes.now_notes: In a developed liberal democracy the adherent supports strategic industrial policy, state investment funds, infrastructure, technical education, tough law and order, national service, limits on disruptive protest, and anti-corruption measures. They favour efficient executive government over gridlock and value outcomes over procedural pluralism.

sources.title: From Third World to First: The Singapore Story 1965–2000
sources.author: Lee Kuan Yew

sources.title: The Country, the Revolution and I
sources.author: Park Chung-hee

sources.title: Asia's Next Giant: South Korea and Late Industrialization
sources.author: Alice H. Amsden

archetypes.name: Neoreaction
archetypes.summary: Prioritises effective, accountable sovereign authority, modelled on a corporation run by a chief executive, and citizens' freedom to exit, over democracy, egalitarianism and a progressive establishment.
archetypes.signature: ideal: patchwork of sovereign corporate city-states run by CEO-monarchs; now: exit, institution-building, and executive power against the bureaucracy
archetypes.brief: Democracy is not a check on power. It hands power to an unaccountable establishment of universities, media and civil service, which we call 'the Cathedral'. Good government is a question of incentives. A sovereign state should be run like a well-managed corporation, with a chief executive accountable to owners or shareholders, a system called neocameralism. Ideally the world becomes a patchwork of many small sovereign states competing for residents. Citizens are customers with the right of exit, not voters with voice. Order and security are the state's product: low crime and high stability. Liberty is the private freedom of a well-run realm, not political participation. Property and markets are respected, and the state itself is property. Trade is pragmatic. Sovereigns avoid crusading wars. Immigration is controlled by the sovereign's interest. Religion is optional and social norms are unpoliced, though many adherents are traditionalists. We are divided by our own 'trichotomy': techno-commercialists, who are accelerationist and pro-technology, religious traditionalists, and ethno-nationalists.
archetypes.now_notes: Here and now the adherent mostly rejects activism. They favour exit: charter cities, startup and network states, and crypto. They build parallel institutions, critique universities and media, and support strengthening executive power over the administrative state, civil-service reform and replacing bureaucrats. Some engage in right-wing politics, while others stay detached.

archetypes.name: Techno-progressive transhumanism
archetypes.summary: Prioritises using science and technology to overcome biological limits, such as ageing, disease and cognitive constraints, with fair access guaranteed by democratic institutions, over bioconservative restraint and 'natural' limits.
archetypes.signature: constant
archetypes.brief: Humanity is a work in progress. Enhancement, life extension, genetic therapy, brain-computer interfaces and advanced AI can free people from suffering and expand human potential. Each person has 'morphological freedom', a right to modify their own body and mind. But technology must not deepen inequality, so we are techno-progressive: democratic institutions, regulation and a strong welfare state should ensure safety and universal access, including publicly funded enhancement and a basic income as automation spreads. We favour liberal democracy and civil liberties, with security measures against catastrophic risks. We favour mixed economies, with public research and planning for frontier technology. Trade and scientific knowledge should flow freely, with risky research coordinated nationally and globally. We are internationalist and favour global governance of AI and biotech risks, and we are dovish. We welcome immigrants and diversity, extended to future persons, uplifted animals and AIs. The state is secular, and our social values are strongly progressive. We are divided with libertarian extropians over markets, and among ourselves over accelerating versus slowing AI for safety.
archetypes.now_notes: Here and now the adherent supports public funding for longevity, gene therapy and AI research, a universal basic income, legalising safe enhancement and cognitive drugs, reproductive and bodily autonomy, AI safety regulation, international science cooperation, and equitable access to new therapies. They work through advocacy groups, research, and progressive parties.

sources.title: Citizen Cyborg: Why Democratic Societies Must Respond to the Redesigned Human of the Future
sources.author: James Hughes

archetypes.name: Critical-rationalist liberalism
archetypes.summary: Prioritises institutions that let a society find and correct its mistakes without violence (removable rulers, criticisable secular laws, piecemeal reform, and a civic culture that keeps them working) over the question of who should rule or a blueprint for the ideal society.
archetypes.signature: ideal: an open society whose rulers and laws can be removed without bloodshed, improved step by step; now: defends the institutions of correction, gradual testable reform and high civic standards
archetypes.brief: All knowledge is fallible, and that includes political knowledge, so the first question is not 'who should rule?' but 'how can we organise institutions so that bad rulers and bad policies do as little harm as possible, and can be got rid of without bloodshed?' That is what democracy is for: not the rule of the people as such, but the peaceful removal of governments and the correction of laws. We favour representative democracy with clear accountability, a free press, independent courts and the rule of law, binding rulers like everyone else. Laws must rest on reasons that anyone can examine and dispute, never on revelation or tradition placed beyond criticism, so church and state are separate. Society should improve by piecemeal social engineering: many small, reversible reforms that fight concrete evils, with each result checked against the problem, rather than utopian redesigns to a plan, which concentrate power, cannot learn from their mistakes and end in violence. Institutions are not enough: they work only where citizens share the habits they depend on, such as honesty, tolerance, respect for rules, willingness to lose an argument or a vote, and high standards of participation and public behaviour, so civic education and standards matter. Tolerance does not extend to movements that reject argument and use or plan violence to destroy the open society (the paradox of tolerance). Economics is settled the same way, by trial and error: most of us favour a market economy with competition, open trade and a state that protects the weak from exploitation, the size of the safety net being a matter for testable reform. We are internationalist: we want an international legal order that restrains aggressors, and we accept force to defend open societies and stop aggression. Newcomers are welcome and should be expected to accept the civic rules of the society they join. We are individualist and socially liberal, and we are optimistic about science and technology, since problems are soluble by new knowledge. We are divided on how much welfare the state should provide, and on how far to go in restricting anti-democratic parties.
archetypes.now_notes: In a present-day liberal democracy the adherent defends the institutions that allow peaceful correction: free and fair elections, independent courts, a free press, scientific freedom and transparent government. They back gradual, evidence-tested reforms (pilots, sunset clauses, evaluation) over sweeping programmes, push for higher standards of civic education and public conduct, support legal limits on movements that organise violence against democracy, favour open trade and Western alliances, and are pro-science and pro-innovation. They oppose populists and revolutionaries alike who place the question of who rules above how rulers can be removed.

notes: Composition check (47 archetypes; the spec says about 44). Family counts: socialist 6, left-liberal 5 (including transhumanism), liberal-centrist 4, conservative 4, religious 6, nationalist-populist 6, libertarian-market 4, anarchist 6, hierarchical 6. Every family has at least 3. Non-Western traditions: African socialism (Ujamaa), Islamic democracy, Gandhian Sarvodaya, Kemalism, Peronism (Latin America), Confucian meritocracy, and developmental authoritarianism (East and Southeast Asia); theocratic absolutism is generic but draws on Islamic and Catholic precedents. Centrist or moderate archetypes: Centrism and Third Way, with social liberalism and constitutional monarchism also moderate, so the 1–2 rule is met or slightly exceeded. Gaps and flags: (1) There is no Indigenous or decolonial archetype; consider an Indigenous sovereignty or decolonial archetype. (2) Buddhist political thought is missing (for example Buddhist economics or Buddhist socialism), and Hindu political traditions appear only through Gandhian Sarvodaya; Hindutva would need the sensitive flag if added. (3) Latin American left traditions beyond Peronism and generic left populism (for example Bolivarian socialism or liberation theology) and pan-Africanism as a standalone archetype are missing. (4) There is no agrarian or peasant populist archetype and no feminist-specific archetype; feminism is arguably cross-cutting. (5) Naming rule: the 'Justicialism' parenthetical (self-name of a living party) was dropped in review; the archetype is now 'Peronism'. Trotskyism, Kemalism, Peronism, Georgism and Gandhian are eponyms of deceased figures, which complies with the no-living-individuals rule. (6) Pairs at risk of near-duplication for the leave-one-coder-out check: social liberalism and progressive liberalism; paleolibertarianism and anarcho-capitalism; Confucian meritocracy and developmental authoritarianism; national conservatism and right-populism; democratic socialism and market socialism. (7) Transhumanism is filed under left-liberal, but its tec pole cuts across families, and libertarian transhumanism is absent. (8) The sensitive pairing follows the spec: fascism is coded historically (interwar Italian model, explicitly excluding National Socialism), and Marxism–Leninism is briefed in its Stalinist variant. Neoreaction and developmental authoritarianism are not flagged sensitive per the input list. Reviewers may want to revisit that symmetrically with absolute monarchism. (9) Several sources are by living authors; this is fine because the naming rule covers archetype names only. URLs are included only where confident (Lenin). Review pass (2026-10-31): briefs extended so each touches all 12 axis topics (fed, dem, lib, col, pla, glo, int, mil, mul, rel, pro, tec); neoliberalism's hostile second critic (Harvey) replaced with the Mont Pelerin Society Statement of Aims so no family carries two critical sources against one by adherents; right-populism's Lasch removed and Lind recoded as non-adherent, with Deneen added as an adherent source; MacIntyre recoded non-adherent (he rejected the communitarian label); transhumanism's extropian source swapped for the Transhumanist Declaration to match the techno-progressive variant; Technocracy Study Course author corrected; a few evaluative or uneven phrasings neutralised (e.g. 'humane immigration system', ML religion policy, Kemalist assimilation of Kurds, Italian Fascist gas campaign in Ethiopia).
